speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am told this bill will have to stand in my name because it deals with the tariff, and I do not propose to move the first reading until the tariff items are all disposed of, which I hope will be done this afternoon. The clerk tells me that should be done before we proceed with the bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend, just for the sake of information, why it is that in this instance we proceed to approve of an agreement by way of a bill which is not preceded by a resolution, whereas in the case of the Statute of Westminster we simply approved of the arrangement and no bill was necessary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In 1927, I think, when the rules were amended, the necessity was removed for preceding a matter of trade by resolution, when it does not involve putting

Australian Trade Agreement
charges upon the people and things of that kind. I am informed by the clerk that this is the rule at present. With respect to the Statute of Westminster we were simply petitioning His Majesty to lay before his parliament certain legislation. In this instance a trade agreement has been arrived at which affects the future of this country, and parliament is being asked to ratify and confirm it, but it does not come into force until proclamations are issued in both countries. The only difficulty is that certain tariff items must be approved of before the bill is read the first time, and the committee on ways and means should have disposed of those tariff items first. I consulted the clerk at the table with respect to the matter, and he advised me that under the practice of this house the bill should not be proceeded with until such time as the tariff items in the agreement had been sanctioned by the committee, following which the bill to confirm the agreement will be introduced.

I understood my right hon. friend to say that if a bill respecting trade and commerce does not place burdens on anyone, under the rules it need not be preceded by a resolution, but I would direct my right hon. friend's attention to the fact that this bill does impose certain tariffs, and since tariffs are in the nature of taxation certainly it imposes burdens on the people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps I should have added to that sentence and said unless the resolutions had been considered by a committee of the house. These resolutions are now before the committee of the house, and the proper course is to take no further step until the committee have completed consideration of the resolutions which were placed in the votes and proceedings the other evening and proceeded with yesterday by consent of the house, for which I thanked the right hon. gentleman yesterday since it enabled us to advance practically all the items. I think there are very few items outstanding; we will dispose of those this afternoon and then take the further step in connection with the bill.
Then I understand that if this bill does not impose any tariffs in addition to those in the general measure there is no need for a resolution.

This affords me an opportunity to say that my right hon. friend's consent is not meeting me at all. It may meet the convenience of the public. When we discussed the question as to the amount of the supply hill, whether one-twelfth or otie-sixth should be passed, the right hon.

Montreal Harbour
gentleman thought that a month was ample, and we acted on that consent. I believe that last year it was made one-sixth, at least on one occasion. I thought that probably the house might hope to prorogue within a week or ten days and it might not be a matter of tremendous importance. But in view of representations made to me this morning as to the situation in city communities, and the undesirability perhaps of credit being asked for, with a possible refusal, I said that I would ask the opposition for their consent to a bill being passed. If the opposition does not desire that it should fee done in the public interest, then I assure them that as far as I am concerned personally, it does not matter because matters of this kind are never matters of personal interest. One who has to discharge a public duty discharges that duty as well as he can. It cannot possibly be considered a matter of accommodation to me, it is a matter of public interest. If it is thought to be in the public interest, and I believe it is, then I ask the right hon. gentleman to agree to its being done, as a matter of public interest and not as an obligement. There is no question of personal accommodation in this matter, and I never took that view while I occupied the position of leader of the opposition.
So far as the future business of the house is concerned, the measures to be dealt with are those arising out of the budget resolutions and those, with I think three exceptions, now before the house. There is a public measure dealing with an amendment to the Red Cross Act. A serious situation has arisen because of the proceedings before a committee of this house. I have not asked the house to agree to morning sittings because that committee is sitting. It is a committee charged with very important duties and in the light of what transpired to-day and with respect to which the government has not yet had an opportunity to consider its future action, it may be that legislation will have to be submitted to this house for the purpose of compelling the attendance of certain witnesses who have declined to attend. The passing of a statute may be necessary or it may be that the matter can be dealt with by a royal commission. I cannot make any statement as to what the future business may be until such time as we have had an opportunity to determine what course of action will be taken in connection with this matter.

may I say to my right hon. friend that when I asked him if he would advise the opposition as to the future business of the house.
I hope he did not think that I was seeking any personal consideration. It was in the public interest and in the interest of all hon. members of the house that I made the request. I know that when the right hon. gentleman asks for interim supply it is not to enable him to get through the rest of the month, but rather for the benefit of the community generally.
May I point out to my right hon. friend that he knows that the fiscal year begins on April 1, and if he were thinking of the public interest he would arrange to have his supply voted before that time, at least for the most part. He can call parliament at any date he likes and he should not have to come to the opposition in order to get his supply put through. I hope another year he will get the session started a little earlier and bring down any important measures earlier in the session, rather than leave them until the last ten days.

subtopic: THE FISHING INDUSTRY OF THE MARITIME . PROVINCES
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to take the time of the house at this late stage of the session, and I would not do so did I not feel it were necessary in the interests of one particular industry in my own province and in the maritime provinces generally. I refer to the fishing industry. Nothing has been said during the present session of the house concerning the plight in which that industry finds itself. We have heard a good deal about the situation of the wheat farmers in western Canada, and rightly so, but their plight is not one bit worse than that of the fishermen scattered along the coast line of the province of Nova Scotia. What is more, these fishermen have had lean years in days gone by and for a considerable period of time, and they have no reserves on which to draw. In order that I may place the question with which I purpose dealing more fully before the house I shall briefly sketch the position of the industry. I am referring particularly to my own province, the province of Nova Scotia, which as hon. members know juts out into the Atlantic. Off the coast of that province are fishing banks equal to any in the world, and fishing communities are scattered along the entire coast line. For more than one hundred years the people of those communities have been going out in their boats and vessels to catch fish. Until recent years the method commonly used for the ground fish, those fish which swim near the bottom of the sea, has been the hook and line. In recent years another instrument of production has been introduced, the steam or otter trawler. The steam or otter trawler
catches fish by drawing a huge purse-shaped net over the floor of the sea, scooping up the fish and hoisting them to its deck.
For some years past the industry has been declining, rather than improving, and for that condition there are a number of contributory causes. Before I give those causes I shall outline a particular illustration of the decline which has taken place in the county of Lunenburg from which I come. In 1918 the port of Lunenburg sent 140 fishing vessels to the banks, each vessel carrying a crew of from 20 to 25 men, earning on an average from SS00 to $1,000 each. This year the number of vessels is reduced to 42 schooners. The number of men on each boat remains about the same, and while the average earnings for this year are not available the average earnings last year were less than $300 per man.
As I have said there are a number of contributory causes not only with reference to Lunenburg but to the whole province, because the decline has been general. In the first place there came the Fordney-McCumber tariff which shut out from the United States a substantial portion of our fish. That situation was further aggravated by the Hawley-Smoot tariff. There has been a world depression which has brought a decline in the price of salt cod fish similar to the decline in the price of wheat. Salt cod fish is sold almost entirely in the export market. This decline has further aggravated the domestic situation because men, vessels and boats which formerly produced entirely for the foreign markets have been driven into the home market. The home market has been unable to absorb the product. Canada in fact is absorbing less than it did in former years, and at greatly reduced prices.
Further than that there is the additional factor of an unsettling controversy which has been raging-and I use the term "raging" advisedly-in Nova Scotia between those who employ the different instruments of production. One may say that the controversy is age old-in a sense it is-but it is one which rages between those who employ the steam or other trawler and those who use the hook and line. The steam or other trawler came to this country from Europe about twenty years ago and was used unsuccessfully in pre-war days. During the war it established a foundation. Most of those however who had fished off our banks during the war returned to their countries. In post-war years however the steam or other trawler has established itself in the province as an instrument of production,
Fishing Industry in Maritimes

and from year to year its numbers vary. At present there are six trawlers operating in the province of Nova Scotia.

friend would know because he is a director of the company controlling them.
I draw this matter to the attention of the house because a controversy has arisen. There are different schools of thought as to what ought to be done. Evidence was given before the royal commission which investigated the maritime fisheries in 1927, and it was so conflicting that it led to both a majority and a minority report. The majority report favoured the abolition of the trawler, but the minority report favoured its retention as an auxiliary instrument of production. The report of the committee gave rise to legislation in this parliament passed in the session of 1929 as an amendment to the Fisheries Act. Section 69a of that act consists altogether of six subsections. In the first place the purport of the section was to place the trawler under licence. Hitherto they had been able to operate freely, but through the legislation there was an effort to compel operation under licences, and only under licences. There was a further provision that such trawlers could not fish within twelve miles of Canadian shores.
There is a fourth provision which I wish particularly to draw to the attention of the house:
(4)	The minister may determine the number *of such vessels that shall be eligible to be licensed.
Then subsection 5 is as follows:
(5)	Regulations may be made under the provisions of section 46 of this act.
(a)	prescribing the form of licences;
(b)	specifying the evidence to be submitted with an application for a licence;
(c)	fixing the conditions under which a licence shall be issued;
(d)	making any other provisions respecting licences.
Under the provisions of subsection 5 an order in council was passed in October, 1929, which imposed certain restrictions which were termed licence fees. I do not purpose to deal with those because payment was resisted, and a case was heard before Mr. Justice Audette
{Mr. Ernst.]
of the exchequer court in which he decided that the order in council is ultra vires, although no reference of course is made to the statute itself being ultra vires. From this decision an appeal has been taken to the Supreme Court of Canada by the crown. My only reason for referring to the case is that the contention may be raised that I am referring to a matter which is sub judice. I do not intend to refer to the question which is before the court, namely the validity of the order in council.
One of the prime reasons for dealing with the question is that the very uncertainty of having the matter before the court is creating an uncertainty in the industry. I feel it is essential to the progress, stability and development of the industry that some measure of policy should be announced, whatever that policy may foe. Under the sections of the act which I have read power remains in the minister by which he may give effect to a fairly broad and moderate policy.
I have outlined the history of the matter so that the question may properly be understood by the house. As I have said there are two schools of thought in the province of Nova Scotia and I feel bound to place them both before hon. members. The constituency from which I oome supports the school of thought which makes representations advocating that the trawler be abolished. They base their representations upon two grounds: First, the conservation of the fisheries and secondly what they call "glutting" the market -a condition to which I shall apply a different term. They say that the trawler destroys the fishing ground and that its use results in over-production. I have placed their views before the hous<5 because I have felt it my duty so to do. Having put those views forward I feel it equally my duty, grave though the responsibility and position may be, to say that I cannot accept them. I do not believe in the abolition of the trawler; I advocate restriction and regulation. With reference to the question of conservation, that can be disposed of very simply by saying it is entirely an International question, and that to restrict or abolish the trawlers of Canada whilst trawlers from other lands can fish on the banks of the high seas would not in any way tend to preserve fish life.
Furthermore, from study which has taken place in the North sea, it is not apparent that the method of production is wrong; it resolves itself simply into a question of the intensity of fishing. I believe the minister would serve a useful purpose to the fisheries of this country if he would endeavour to have

Fishing Industry in Maritimes
an international convention called to deal with the question of conservation, so that there will not be depletion, and further to deal with what is even more important, the question of the destruction of fishing gear. I brought to the attention of this house this session one instance of apparently wanton and deliberate destruction of the gear of a fishing vessel by a French trawler. Such instances are not by any means uncommon, and any international arrangement which could be brought about tending to eliminate that practice would be to the advantage of those who use line fishing.
With reference to the "glutting" of the market, that resolves itself into a question of production. Undoubtedly many of our own fishermen have had to turn from the salt fish field to the fresh fish field, either wholly or in part, which has contributed to that condition. I feel that this fault, if it be a fault, does not call for abolition but for restriction and regulation.
I come now to the arguments of those who advocate unlimited trawling. In the first place they say it is an economic development and that you cannot Stop the machine. May I say, sir, that usually with such economic developments cheapness of production is a prime essential. From the evidence given by those who own the trawlers there is no indication that they are cheapening production costs; their chief argument is not cheap production but continuity of supply, with which I propose to deal in a few moments. Even if this were an economic change bound to take place, in view of present conditions and in view of the fact that thousands of these men. scattered along the coast line, are ill-adapted for any other calling, such economic change should be slowed and regulated in *order to cause as little dislocation as possible to those now engaged in the industry.
With reference to continuity of supply I may say that in part I accept that argument of those who advocate trawling. Continuity of supply, I am convinced as the result of four years of careful study, cannot be maintained without some use of the trawler. True it is that conditions have changed as they affect those who fish with boats and particularly with vessels. They no longer depend on sails; they are powered with crude oil engines, but still there are times of storm when the dory cannot be put over the side, and the fish are not forthcoming. In the present state of the fish market those who purchase fish, particularly in central Canada, insist upon fresh rather than frozen fish, and the result is that during the last winter there
have been instances, as probably there will be instances during the coming winter, when the trawler was essential to maintain that continuity of supply which is necessary for the development and maintenance of market.
Having stated that I accept that argument, may I indicate one other circumstance which is aggravating the situation. As I have stated, there are six trawlers under licence at the moment in the province of Nova Scotia, of which the greater proportion are under the control of one corporation. Under the restrictions brought in by the previous government there is positive prohibition against bringing in further trawlers from outside. To build them at home would entail many times the cost of those already under licence, because they were imported from abroad. In addition, in the present uncertain state of affairs, no one would want to bring in a trawler even if he could do so. The result is a virtual monopoly by that one corporation. I am not finding fault with the corporation; this condition has been an accident, but it should not be allowed to continue, because it can result in only one thing. The firm which employs this mechanical instrument of production will gradually squeeze out of existence all the smaller fish firms scattered along the coast of the province, the fishermen who live in those localities where the smaller concerns operate will be deprived of their local market, and the last stage of the industry will be worse than the first.
You may ask what I advocate. I advocate a middle course. I believe that compromise will provide the solution, and I am going to venture to read one paragraph of a letter written by a gentleman with whom I very seldom agree but with whom, in this instance, I agree very cordially. I refer to the hon. member for Antigonish^Guysborough (Mr. Duff). This letter appeared in the Halifax Chronicle of September 5, 1909, dealing with this very question:
Before closing may I say that although the arguments on this question are nearly all, if not all, in favour of the real fishermen of Nova Scotia, yet the question must be dealt with by practical men in a sane and sensible manner and with a view to protecting as far as possible any vested interests by endeavouring to compose the present extreme differences between the line fishermen and the steam trawlers. My experience in life has taught me that it is necessary and usually the best policy to compromise where the opinions of two opposing parties are diametrically opposite and to endeavour to find a means of mutual agreement which will partially satisfy both parties. This question is of such a grave nature that there should not be any arbitrary or hasty judgment made.
Fishing Industry in Maritimes

Well, Mr. Speaker, no arbitrary or hasty judgment has been given, because that letter was written almost two years ago. I say, as I have stated previously, that I favour restriction and regulation, and I desire to put forward some suggestions to the minister in the hope that at least some of them may meet with his approval.
In the first place I do not believe any trawler should operate out of the ports of Canada, or bring fish into the ports of Canada to be landed here, except under licence by the crown. I make that statement because I believe first of all there should be the element of control. The licence fee, of course, is a question for government determination an accordance with the ability of the industry to pay.
In the second place I do not believe there should be any increase in the number of trawlers operating at present; in fact I believe there should be a decrease, and that no one firm or corporation should be allowed to operate more trawlers than are absolutely necessary to insure continuity of supply. That is, the trawler should be used as an auxiliary aid to the vessel and the boat fishermen, because I am confident that if this policy is adopted, and the minister requires that he be satisfied before issuing a licence that it is solely for the purpose of enabling continuity of supply to be maintained, no firm will control or operate a large portion of the trawlers operating in the province of Nova Scotia. In fact I feel that this monopoly is one of the things which must be got rid of if the other firms are to survive. Under the section of the act which I have read undoubtedly the minister now has power to do both the things I have advocated, because the act itself was not called into question before the courts; only the order in council was attacked. Subsection 4 of section 69 (a) states that the minister may determine the number of such vessels that shall be eligible to be licensed, the word "vessel" in that instance referring to the trawler. Subsection 5 states:
Regulations may be made under the provisions of section forty-six of this act,-
(a)	prescribing the form of licence;
(b)	specifying the evidence to be submitted with an application for a licence;
(c)	fixing the conditions under which a licence shall be issued;
(d)	making any other provisions respecting licences.
Now, sir, I wish to put forward a further view, which I grant is a personal view rather difficult of attainment, because it conflicts with vested interests. It is my own contention that no trawler should be eligible for

licence unless it has been built within Canada. I so contend because these ships with which the trawlers compete are built in Canada and at Canadian prices. The trawlers are purchased mainly in England, where they are tied up at wharves or fish piers, and they are purchased at prices which in this country practically amount to dumping. They are then brought in to compete with our vessels.
I contend that it would be thoroughly in keeping with the policies of the Conservative party to accept the trawler as an implement of production under licence, but only when it is built in Canada from Canadian steel and with Canadian labour. This would give very much needed employment to Canadian workmen and shipyards. It would raise this further question:	What are you to do with
those which are here? Speaking altogether personally, I would suggest that they be sold and that the owners be reimbursed for any loss they might sustain; and I would make arrangements to have Canadian trawlers built. If I am asked why I make such a proposal, the answer is that I am convinced of the necessity for restriction. I have no doubt that the cost of building in Canada would impose sufficient restrictions to prevent the over-rapid development of a trawler fleet.
I put forward that view knowing that it involves difficulties and that it conflicts with vested interests. I realize that it is practically a confiscation of vested interests that have accrued in years gone by. If my view is not acceptable, however, I urge that for the future, having licensed those now in Canada, we license no more trawlers unless they are built in this country. This, as I have pointed out, would give work to Canadian labour and to our Canadian shipyards. When I make this suggestion I am conscious of treading on thorny ground. It will be immediately urged by those who are interested in the trawler companies that in advocating the interests of Lunenburg I am taking away markets which others have spent years in building up. In reply to that contention I say that in the first place, admitting that the markets in Canada for fish have been built up by corporations which to-day use the trawler, this has not been done without substantial government assistance in the way of plaints, marketing and advertising. And in the years gone by assistance has also been given in the way of bonus on freight rates. In the second place, let me point out that I am not advocating the interests of Lunenburg alone. Anyone who will visit Nova Scotia to-day will realize what a live question this is in fishing communities. The only districts I know of which do not support

Fishing Industry in Maritimes
abolition are Halifax and Digby; in almost every other section of the province abolition is demanded. Perhaps I am taking my political life in my hands in saying that I do not agree with them, but certainly I am not advocating the interests of Lunenburg alone. Even if I were, however, my county is dependent upon fishing. The industry has built up the county and maintained prosperity not only in the fishing communities but in the back country where the wood is obtained for building the vessels. And I should be doing a disservice to my county if, in order to protect interests in Halifax or elsewhere, I were willing to sacrifice those among whom I was bom and brought up.
I have made my case as moderately as possible and as fairly as I can, in an absolutely non-partisan spirit but in the sincere hope that some announcement of policy will be made which will give the industry some idea of what it can look forward to in the future, and so that it can make its plans accordingly. I should like to see this problem solved for it is causing great unrest and agitation in Nova Scotia.
I know quite well that I have dealt- with but one problem of the fishing industry, but it is more immediate and urgent than any other. What I am proposing is by no means a panacea for all the ills of the fishing industry; there are a dozen other problems that must be solved. But I put forward this particular [DOT]one because of its urgency. The condition of the industry is grave; it has never been more so. I want to thank the Prime Minister for restoring to the exempted list under the sales tax articles purchased by the fishermen. It [DOT]may not seem much, but even a slight straw sometimes will break the camel's back. I can assure him that the fishermen of my constituency appreciate his action. I am not speaking in any spirit of pessimism with regard to this industiy. I believe it has a future far greater than its past would lead us to expect. And I have no doubt that, with wise development, the industry in the future can take care of far more capital and a greater number of men than it can do to-day. It is because of this conviction that I have presumed to take up the time of the house to bring before it this problem which is of so much importance to the people whom I represent.

subtopic: THE FISHING INDUSTRY OF THE MARITIME . PROVINCES
speechtext:
I
am surprised that my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg should bring up this contentious matter at this late time in the session. This trawler question is a very live one, having been before the house for the last four
or five years. It was dealt with thoroughly by the committee in 1929, and as a result of their deliberations there was presented to the house and passed Bill No. 26 which proved perfectly satisfactory both to the trawler industry and to the fishermen. Had the regulations under that bill been carried out there would have been no difficulty on either side, either on the part of the shore fishermen or so far as the trawlers are concerned. But for some reason or other a commission was appointed to look into the situation and it made a recommendation. It was on their recommendation that Bill No. 26 was based.
Now, all the regulations provided for in that bill cover the objections made by my hon. friend to the trawlers. The regulations limit the number of trawlers that may be used, and that is left entirely to the discretion of the minister. The minister is empowered to collect a licence fee from the trawlers, and as I said before, the bill was satisfactory both to the fishermen and to the trawler interests. My hon. friend's constituency now comes forward with representations. The fishermen there are not shore fishermen; they are offshore fishermen, owners and operators of large schooners. It was not the shore fishermen who started this agitation of late. They are satisfied now with the way conditions are working. The trawler companies have been their best market for fish. There would never have been any trawlers operating in Nova Scotia if it were not absolutely essential to have them in the fishing business, to provide a regular supply of fish for the markets of the country. Prior to 1910, when the first trawler came to Nova Scotia, there was no fresh fish market in Canada. The supply all came from Boston and Portland; not a thousand pounds of fresh fish per week were shipped to the upper provinces from Nova Scotia. The government at about that time gave a rebate on the express charges amounting to one-third of the cost in order to try to build up a fresh fish business with the upper provinces. That was the beginning of the fresh fish business in this country. Previous to that practically every pound of fish was brought in from Boston because we could not supply the market with fish when it was required. When the trawler was brought into operation it was then possible to supply fish as required and the result is that a very successful fresh fish business has been built up. This business has been built up by the steam trawlers. These trawler companies buy from one-third to two-thirds of the catch from the boat fishermen, as is shown by the report of the commission which investigated the fish-

Fishing Industry in Maritimes
eries in 1928. Now that the trawler companies have built up a successful business, the vessel owners of the county of Lunenburg want to step in and reap the benefit. Both money and time has been expended by the trawler companies in the development of markets; they have spent years in working up this trade which is being endangered by agitation coming now almost entirely from the county of Lunenburg.
I live in a fishing county where not a single trawler is operated, but we have the best class of shore fishermen in Digby county that there is in the province of Nova Scotia. They operate the very best class of boats, but they have no objection to the trawler because they realize that a regular supply of fish is necessary to hold the market. My hon. friend has stated that modern vessels equipped with engines are being used. I want to tell him that in 1910 a fleet of vessels was operating out of the port of Digby. These vessels were equipped with engines, perhaps not as powerful as those used to-day, but I submit that an engine in a vessel has nothing to do with catching fish. In order to catch fish the men are obliged to go out in small boats in order to set their trawls and there are weeks at a time when it is impossible to put a small boat over the side. When the commission was sitting in Lockeport in 1928 it was shown that for four weeks there had not been a single fish landed by a schooner.
Is this modern industry worth millions of dollars, using modem methods of production, to be ruined in order that we may go back to line fishing? That would be a great mistake to make, and the business people of this country would not stand for it. My hon. friend is mistaken when he says that all these trawlers are operated by one company. Four trawlers are owned and operated by the company of which I have the honour to be a member. I take some credit to myself for the building up of the fish industry. When I was in business for myself I shipped the first carload of finnan haddie which ever went to the west, and from that beginning a great business has developed. The business carried on at Lunenburg has always been a salt fish business. It has not been so successful dining the past few years and they want to convert it to a fresh fish business. They ask that the trawler be abolished in order that they may gain control of the markets of this country. What my hon. friend has said might have been said to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and to the department, and I presume he has taken that course. He has brought 
this matter up in the house simply because he represents a fishing constituency. I represent a fishing constituency but the interests who own fishing vessels in my hon. friend's constituency have told him that he must bring this matter up on the floor of the House of Commons, and that is the reason why he has done so.

speechtext:
I have no objection to stating that I am interested in the trawler business, and I am proud of it. If it had not been for the trawlers, there would be no fresh fish markets for the Canadian fishermen. Our company has done more for the shore fishermen Of Nova Scotia than any other half dozen concerns.
My hon. friend brought up the question of conservation. Six small trawlers only operate out of the province of Nova Scotia and according to regulations they cannot fish within twelve miles of the shore. During the summer months we have from forty to fifty French trawlers, each one four or five times the size of our trawlers, fishing off our banks. The American fleet consists of some 179

Fishing Industry in Maritimes
trawlers, and they fish our banks. It is perfectly ridiculous to say that there is a neea for conservation because of the trawlers operating out of Nova Scotia. If the countries of the world would agree to abolish trawlers as a means of fishing, I would be agreeable, but so long as other countries use that method of fishing, surely Canada is not to be denied the same right.
Another matter brought up by my hon. friend was the destruction of gear. I do not think a single case has been reported where a Canadian trawler has interfered with the gear of our banks fishermen; such damage has been caused by the foreign trawlers. Our captains are familiar with conditions and they take great care not to fish in close proximity to the vessels or to interfere with their gear.
My hon. friend stated that the vessel owners were prepared to ask for legislation to deny to trawlers the right to come to our shores to fish. No one wants that. Everybody realizes that there is a limitation to the trawling industry and I believe at the present time we have all the trawlers necessary to supply the demand of the market, which is all any one should desire. There is a trawler owned by a firm in Lunenburg, with which firm the hon. member for that constituency is in close touch. They built and own a trawler, but they could not operate her successfully with the result that she is lying tied up at her wharf. Four or five years ago they were not against trawling, but when they found they were operating something about which they knew nothing and which they could not operate successfully, they tied her up and said: All those people who are in thi3 business must adopt our antiquated method of catching fish. That is the whole situation. I think it is a great mistake to bring this matter before the house. It is at present before the courts, and until a decision is rendered in connection with a case that was brought before the exchequer court and that has now been appealled before the full bench, no legislation can be passed by the house in connection with the trawling industry. Therefore I think my hon. friend was ill-advised in bringing the matter before the house.

I do not think I can quite agree with the hon member for Digby-Annapolis, (Mr. Short), who has just taken his seat, that this question should not have been brought up. Parliament has now been in session for more than four months, and yet the very large and important industry of fishing has received no consideration whatever by the house. The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) has made out a good case on behalf of the fishermen of his district, but I think my good friend, who is chairman of the fisheries committee, has been a little lax in his duty in not calling that committee together. If the fishing industry

of the Dominion is as important as he and also the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis would lead us to believe, why was the fisheries committee not called together so that important questions in connection with the fishing industry might be discussed, my hon. friend has left it to the very last days of the session to bring this matter before the house.

The hon. member is chairman of the fisheries committee and it is his duty. That committee was appointed by the house early in the session to deal with matters concerning fisheries and not one meeting has been held.

There was one that dealt with marine matters, but there has not been a meeting that dealt with fisheries. I think it is only fair to point this out. There are large questions that could have been discussed regarding the fisheries. While my constituency could not be called altogether a fishing .one, still that industry is of importance in my district and we have many questions that we should like to bring before the committee. Resolutions were passed by the fishermen's association asking for assistance in connection with collecting boats so that our live lobsters plight be put on the markets of the world in competition with those from other parts. This little request from the fishermen of my constituency was denied while, I think, in Nova Scotia assistance is given in this way. This is one matter that could have been taken up and discussed in the fisheries committee.
The question of trawlers is also one that should be discussed. My hon. friend says that it is still before the courts. It was before the courts and they have given a decision. Early in the session I put a question on the order paper asking what tax had been collected and what was still outstanding.

subtopic: THE FISHING INDUSTRY OF THE MARITIME . PROVINCES
speechtext: The case has been appealed; it is still before the courts.

subtopic: THE FISHING INDUSTRY OF THE MARITIME . PROVINCES
speechtext:
I know that. There is a large amount of tax outstanding, and the government does not know whether it is in a position to collect that tax or not until, I suppose, the case is finally decided by the appeal court. But there are many questions that could be brought forward. During every session that I have been a member of the house the fisheries committee has been one of

the important committees. Representations have been made before it by members from all parts of the maritimes and British Columbia; those questions have been thoroughly discussed and representations have been made to the minister. At the present time our genial friend, the former Premier of Nova Scotia, is Minister of Fisheries, and I know he would be only too glad to have suggestions from members on both sides in connection with the fishing industry. I believe his sole ambition is to give to that industry every assistance he possibly can. How is he to get that information unless members representing the different constituencies meet in the fisheries committee and discuss these matters? It is impossible for him to secure that information through his deputy or any of the officials. The viewpoints of the people in the different constituencies can be stated only by the members representing them.
The trawler question is a big one, and some action should be taken. If it comes to a question between the trawlers and the inshore fishermen, I am for the inshore fishermen every time. If it can be shown that the trawler has a part to play in the fishing industry of Nova Scotia, some restrictions should be put upon its use and the inshore fishermen be given a chance. I think my good friend from Queens-Lunenburg has done a service to this country in bringing the matter before the house, but I do wish to say to him that he should have called the fisheries committee together this session and have given it a chance to discuss these very important questions before they were brought up in the house.
There has been legislation put through the house regarding the tariff, and in that connection I have a clipping here from the Halifax Chronicle, which I think is well worth reading. It says:
The Prime Minister of Canada stated from a hundred platforms that he would make the tariff "fight for the consumer." He repeated in parliament when he imposed new, higher taxes that the people would not have to pay more. How putting 50 cents a garment on the fisherman's oilskins is not going to cost him more, we would like to know. How putting a dollar odd on a dozen pairs of socks is not going to make them cost 12 or 13 cents more a pair, everybody would like to know. How putting a tax on fertilizer, spraying machines, farm machinery and all the rest of it is not going to cost the buyer a cent more, who can explain?
It goes on to deal with the question of falling prices of world commodities and claims that some consideration should be given to the fishermen.
I hope that if we are spared to see another session our good fniend from Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Ernst) will call the fisheries committee together early in the session and give us a chance to discuss the situation from A to Z, so that we may be in a position to put before the minister any recommendations that we may decide upon in connection with these matters. There are very many questions to be considered. There is the protection service, which has always been a contentious question, and I believe that in our province to-day that service has not been handled in a way that is altogether satisfactory to the people there. They feel that the fishermen who live there should be engaged in the work rather than have outside men come in to do it. But I am not going to interfere in that matter, because it is a question of policy for the minister and for the department, and the minister can carry out that policy as he sees fit. In closing, I trust that the fisheries committee will be called together early next session and be given a chance to discuss these matters before they are brought up on the floor of the house.

Mr. Speaker, at this late stage of
the session, having in mind the desire on the part of hon. members of this house to bring about a speedy termination of its business,
I trust that my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst), the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis (Mr. Short), and the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) will not consider me guilty of any discourtesy if I do not discuss this question at any great length, nor is the comparative brevity of my remarks to be taken as in any way an indication of a lack of appreciation on my part of the very grave character of the subject matter which has been brought to the attention of the house by my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg,
May I say at the very outset, and I say it in the kindliest way possible, that I am rather sorry that my hon. friend from Prince, even in a mild way, has injected an element of controversy into the discussion which I think had better be absent, and for this reason:	The matter brought to the attention
of the house Hy the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg dealt solely with the question of trawlers. He left all other questions dealing with fisheries to one side. The trawler question, of all questions, is one which ought not to be made the subject of political party controversy. It is a very serious and difficult question, and I may say frankly that it
15, 1931
Fishing Industry in Maritimes
has given me very great concern, and I have given a very great deal of thought and attention and consideration to the subject. I think that perhaps we had an example in the house this afternoon, in the attitudes that were taken by two hon. members on this side of the house, which indicates that the subject is not one free from difficulties.
I take no exception whatsoever to the fact that this subject has been brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. I think perhaps my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis did not hear, or certainly did not follow, the trend of the remarks of the hon. member who introduced this subject, because my hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg in a very reasonable, very fair and very mild manner was at pains to indicate the conflicting interests as between the trawlers on the one hand and the line fishermen upon the other.
One of the greatest difficulties that we have in considering this question arises out of a number of collateral circumstances. In the first place, a marked change has taken place in the character of the fishing industry in Nova Scotia. The very backbone of that industry was for many years the salt fish industry, but owing to world conditions that I shall not enter into at the moment, inroads have been made upon that business and prices have fallen to inordinately low levels, in some oases to below the cost of production. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg has very properly stated that the fishermen were driven into the fresh fish business on the Canadian market, which is very limited at best.
When the royal commission presided over by Mr. Justice MacLean sat in 1928 they found a very serious condition in the industry. They recognized the difficulties of the trawler situation at the time. It is unfortunate-I say this with every respecl^-that that commission could not have arrived at a unanimous decision by means of a compromise. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg has referred to a letter published in the Halifax Chronicle quoting the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysfoorough (Mr. Duff). In the letter in question, which was published' in the Halifax Chronicle of September 25, 1929, he takes that very position. I am not going to take the time of the house to read a paragraph or two of that letter, which I have before me at the moment, but he expresses in no uncertain terms his regret that the commission could not have compromised and arrived at a unanimous decision.

This is what happened. The majority of the members of that commission recommended the abolition of the trawler. One member, Mr. Justice MacLean, the chairman, took the opposite point of view. I think the late government made a mistake-I do not for a moment wish tio be understood as finding any fault in the sense of political party controversy-when they did not follow the recommendation of their own commission, or of the majority. What they did was to attempt to meet the situation by order in council, which got them nowhere. In the first place the majority of that commission recommended abolition of the tratwier, whereas the order in council itself was predicated upon the operation of the trawlers. Furthermore, while for nine months of the year fish brought into this country by Canadian vessels for the Canadian market, was to be taxed one cent per pound, although that tax was tentatively imposed under the guise of a so-called licence fee, yet at the same time under that order in council the government allowed fish to come in during the months of January, February and March, thus recognizing in the very body of the order in council the contention of those who advocated the use of the trawler; namely, that there are certain periods of inclement weather when we must have trawler-caught fish if we are going to have a continuous supply in the Canadian market. Furthermore, another very unfortunate circumstance resulted from the passing of that order in council, namely, that if the order in council was constitutional it imposed a tax upon one company alone of between 8130,000 and
8150,000	a year, or, as the books of the company disclosed, an amount sufficient to involve a very large deficit in every operating year. In other words, the company could not continue to operate. It is true that it refused to pay the tax and resisted to the extent of fighting the case in the courts. Unfortunately it was unable to finance and its failure recoiled upon the heads of the very fishermen who felt hostile towards the trawler, or those fishermen who believed that the trawler was in large measure responsible for the conditions in which they found themselves. The royal commission found that in the year 1926, which was apparently the last year for which figures were available, 90,000,000 pounds of fish were caught in the province of Nova Scotia. Of that 90,000,000 pounds 40,000,000 were caught by the trawlers and 50,000,000 by the line fishermen. Of the 50,000,000 pounds caught by the line fishermen, however, 72 per cent were purchased from them for cash by the trawler companies. Therefore to the extent that the financial operations of trawler IMr. Rhodes.!
companies were crippled; by the order in council, to that extent was limited the purchasing power of the people of Canada to buy fish caught by line fishermen. Instead of operating as a help to fishermen the order in council recoiled upon their heads. Although I am prepared to give credit to the government of the day for proper motives in passing the order in council, it is an unfortunate fact that it recoiled upon the heads of the fishermen for whose benefit it was designed, to the extent that it prevented the companies from being assured of a future in the business and lessened their chances of operating. To that extent it crippled their opportunities to buy fish from the fishermen of the province of Nova Scotia.
I do not purpose to go into the merits of this matter at length, but there are one or two factors to which I think particular attention should be called and which ought to be borne in mind. This controversy is not new. Trawler fishing has been in existence for a hundred years, and the very agitation which we have had to-day in portions of Canada as a result of trawler operations is an old story in practically every country-well, probably not every country, but in a large number of the countries of the world. The mother country was faced with a similar condition and as a result there were numerous royal commissions and inquiries. Investigations have been held in the United States, but there has never been any demand in any of the different countries to abolish the trawler. In Canada we have just off the shores of the province of Nova Scotia, where this agitation is most acute, what is perhaps one of the greatest fishing grounds in the world. other markets of Ontario, will not take other than fresh fish. This is made very clear by the evidence of Mr. Langskill, who is associated with the fish distribution business in Toronto. He said:
I have seen a fresh Atlantic fish business in Toronto develop from a few cases weekly to several carloads per week due to the development of the trawler assuring us of a steady supply.
He referred to an incident which happened only last year, and stated that owing to the inclement weather off the Atlantic coast lie would not have been able to supply his market but for the fact that he was able to get fresh fish caught by trawlers.
In any case it was my intention to have made an announcement as to my view and as to the policy of the government with respect to this matter at a reasonably early date. That I have not done so hitherto is very largely because of the fact that, very shortly after coming into office, I realized that we were not beginning to exploit our market possibilities for fish in Canada. If we increased the per capita consumption of fish by 10 pounds per person per year we would increase our market by over 100,000,000 pounds of fish yearly. Even if we arrived at that figure, which is by no means fantastic, we would be still consuming less than three-quarters of the per capita consumption of fish in the mother country, where the people are essentially meat eating people. It is true there are problems in our industry which are peculiar to Canada. We have a country covering half a continent, yet our population is only slightly larger than that of the city of London, and our problem of distribution is a very difficult one because fish is a highly perishable commodity. Realizing this, and with the view of enlarging the Canadian market, the department employed the firm of Cockfield, Brown and Company of Montreal, who were recommended to me as the best firm we could engage in Canada, to undertake under their research engineer a survey of the market possibilities in Canada and the other countries of the world with a view to our being able, as far as governmental activity permitted it to be done, to inaugurate such policies as would enable us to overtake as rapidly as possible that consumption of 100,000,000 pounds or more yearlv. If we were able to do that we would go a very long way towards improving conditions among the fishermen and in the fishing industry.
I am satisfied, and I wish to state very clearly that I accept it as beyond reasonable

doubt at least, that if we are to enlarge our production of fish in Canada to cover this market, and to supply large quantities to the United States, we must have the trawler as an adjunct to our industry in order to take up the slack of which I have spoken.
I do not propose to labour the subject further, because I have already taken more time than I would wish at this stage of the session, but I should like to say this: My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) and myself are practically in entire agreement.
I believe the trawlers should be limited to the irreducible minimum, and should be subject to strict regulations. I think the six we have at the present time are ample, and perhaps too many, but whether or not that is so I believe they should be limited to the lowest possible number. My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg referred to the fact that one of the great complaints was that there was a monopoly in connection with the trawlers. That is so, and in large part it arose through accidental circumstances and not through any desire to create such a condition. This has been the cause of very hard feelings in certain sections of Nova Scotia. Under section 69 (a) of the act the Minister of Fisheries has very wide powers. I sometimes wish they were not quite so wide, because it would take a superman to administer that department in a way which would be reasonably acceptable to the majority of those engaged in the fishing industry. But I do believe that the Minister of Fisheries, under that section of the act and under the regulations which he can invoke, has sufficient power to be able to remedy that situation, if not fully at least in very large part. It will be endeavour to see if some solution cannot be found which will bring about a little more equitable distribution of the trawlers. In that connection I might point out that one of the witnesses who appeared at the hearing of which I have spoken was Captain Myhre, who undoubtedly is well known to my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). He appeared against the trawler, but strange to say, in his evidence, to which I will not refer now, he stated that he had a particular customer who wanted fish on a certain day and that he was unable to supply his customer because the elements did not permit the fishermen to work on that occasion. He said very frankly that it would be of distinct advantage to him, and would permit him to supply his best customers with fish whenever they required it, if he could secure a trawler to take care of

the period when the line fishermen could not secure the necessary supplies.
My hon. friend from Queens-Lunenburg said that he advocated the licensing only of trawlers built in Canada. I will agree with him, with this limitation:	I do not believe
it would be fair to apply that principle in Canada now, since of the six trawlers under licence four were imported from the mother country. They were imported in good faith and were purchased at a considerably higher price than that for which they could be purchased to-day. In addition to the cost, they have expended large sums of money on repairs. In one instance twice as much money was expended in repairs on one trawler as was paid for the trawler originally. Are we prepared to pass legislation confiscatory in its character? If we pass a regulation to provide that all trawlers shall be built in Canada and those now here be disposed of, the government will have to compensate. And if we compensate we hand over to the trawler companies an equivalent sum of money which they will turn around and place in Canadian trawlers. So that we put them in no better position, nor do we improve the condition of the fishing industry. A fairer method would be to license the trawlers we now have, deciding that hereafter any trawler to be licensed1 must be built and owned in Canada. I may say to my hon. friend that, with that reservation, I am prepared to recommend to my colleagues in the government that as a matter of policy this be adopted with regard to the trawler question.

This is one of those items

This is about as good an illustration as we can get of the ease with which tariffs can be raised by putting them on a specific basis. I have here a sample of Japanese silk on which, under the new rate, the duty will be 116 per cent of the value of the silk. The silk is worth only 14 cents a yard, and when you add 10 cents a yard to the 46 per cent you have increased the duty to 116 per cent of the value of the product. An lion. MEMBER:	We cannot see it.
Hold it up.

Here it is. I think this is
a good illustration, I will not say of deliberate deceit, because I do not think it was done deliberately for that purpose, but of the ease with which people can be deceived when you change from a specific to an ad valorem rate. If you told people that you had increased the rate to 116 per cent they would not stand for it; but when you say that 10 cents a yard is added to the 45 per cent they do not regard it as so much until they figure it out. But what is the effect? I have the index figures of prices of silk for September, 1929, September, 1930, and June, 1931. The September, 1929, figure was 77; the September, 1930, figure was 60-9; and in June, 1931, the figure was 66-5, showing a slight increase since last September. In regard to the prices for the last three months of the raw product as compared with the finished silk, we find that the price of raw silk has declined from 43-6 to 36-6 since the first of April, while the price of the finished product has increased from 46-9 to 56-5. This would indicate that the silk manufacturers
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.)
are not suffering from any great reduction in prices. According to the figures given by my right hon. friend, the industry pays in wages 22 per cent of its total income. The tariff protection, taking the average rate on all silk goods-because you cannot discriminate between some goods and others given in the returns-was 29 per cent in 1929 on all imports. And on top of all that we find an American who has a controlling interest in a silk factory in Canada coming and asking-

He had one factory as
against twenty-three. I endeavoured the other evening to make clear what the facts were. The hon. gentleman has taken as an illustration silk valued at 14 cents a yard. If he had followed me he would have observed that the importations amounted to 8,000,000 yards valued for duty purposes at slightly over 50 cents. So that the average of the importations was over 50 cents a yard-approximately 52. The illustration which he takes of 14 cents a yard is hardly a fair one upon which to base a conclusion, and the figures which he gives of average costs in 1929, 1930 and 1931 are themselves conclusive against his contention, to say nothing of the figures he gave with regard to prices during the last three months. I will not go over the ground I traversed the other evening. I said that the gentleman in question had stayed here but a short time, and he did not come for the specific purpose my hon. friend suggests. He was interested as a shareholder and he told me of the conditions in the United States. As I said,_ a brief had previously been filed, and the information he gave me squared with the facts we had. He told me what their experience had been and I found that also to be true. I believed that there was nothing left for us to do, in view of the competition from sur-

plus inventories, but to take the action we did. And that action we took for the reasons I explained at length the other night. My right hon. friend objects to my taking as an illustration the cheapest silk at 14 cents a yard. He says I should take into account the higher priced silks.
